(a) In General.—Chapter 11 of title 14, United States Code, is amended by striking section 293 and inserting the following:“§ 293. Compulsory retirement“(a) Regular Commissioned Officers.—Any regular commissioned officer, except a commissioned warrant officer, serving in a grade below rear admiral (lower half) shall be retired on the 
first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 62 years of age.“(b) Flag-Officer Grades.—(1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), any regular commissioned officer serving in a grade of rear admiral (lower half) or above shall be retired on the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 64 years of age.“(2) The retirement of an officer under paragraph (1) may be deferred—“(A) by the President, but such a deferment may not extend beyond the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 68 years of age; or“(B) by the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating, but such a deferment may not extend beyond the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 66 years of age.”
. 
    (b) Clerical Amendment.—The analysis at the beginning of such chapter is amended by striking the item relating to such section and inserting the following:

“293. 
Compulsory retirement.”.

fable.w: The section sets compulsory retirement ages for Coast Guard officers and lets the President or the Secretary defer retirement. One could be tempted to treat the deferral decision as a procedural step involving participation, but every actor (the President, the Secretary, the officers) is inside the federal government. There is no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving any outside party.

qwen_block.w: This section establishes mandatory retirement ages for federal military officers. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by any party outside the federal government in a decision-making process. The actors involved are federal officials (the President, the Secretary) and federal employees (commissioned officers).
qwen_block.s: Any regular commissioned officer... shall be retired on the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 62 years of age.

opus.w: This section sets mandatory retirement ages for Coast Guard officers. It lets the President or the Secretary defer an officer's retirement. Everyone involved is a federal official or employee, and no outside party is consulted or given a role in the decision. The deferral power may look like a decision process, but it never brings in anyone from outside the federal government, so it is not participation.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes mandatory retirement ages for Coast Guard officers and grants specific federal officials (the President and the Secretary) the authority to defer retirement. All actors involved in these decisions are inside the federal government. There is no requirement for consultation with, or participation by, any outside parties such as the public, states, or non-federal experts.
qwen_chat.s: (2) The retirement of an officer under paragraph (1) may be deferred—(A) by the President, but such a deferment may not extend beyond the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 68 years of age; or(B) by the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating, but such a deferment may not extend beyond the first day of the month following the month in which the officer becomes 66 years of age.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the President or Secretary deferring retirement involves a decision where outside parties could petition or participate. However, the text itself only describes the internal authority of federal officials (President, Secretary) to make these decisions. There is no mention of public comment, advisory boards with non-federal members, consultation with states/tribes, or rights to sue. The actors involved are entirely within the federal government.
